Gil doesn’t collect, share or sell personal data. There’s no account and no server, and the app doesn’t ask for the internet permission.
What the app keeps on your phone

Your learning record: finished lessons, review schedules and results, mistakes, saved words and daily study time.

Settings: daily goal, reminder times, theme, accent and speed, the Hangul sound guide and whether you finished the introduction.

A lesson you left halfway, so that you can continue it later.

You can erase your learning record in Settings. Clearing the app’s storage in your phone’s settings, or uninstalling the app, deletes all of it.

Speaking steps ask for the microphone so that you can record yourself and listen back. A recording is at most 10 seconds long, stays in memory and is never written to storage. It’s gone when you move to the next step or leave the lesson. Without the permission, the rest of the app works as usual.
The app reads English aloud with the text-to-speech engine on your phone and gives it only the lesson’s text. Reminders are scheduled on the phone and shown as notifications.

If Android backup is on for your Google account, Android may include your record and settings in that backup and restore them on a new phone. Google runs this backup under its own terms, and the developer has no access to it. You can turn it off in your phone’s settings.\n\nIn Back up and restore you can also save your record, daily goal, reminder times and settings to a file in a place you choose, and restore them from that file later. The app reads and writes only the file you pick and doesn’t send it anywhere.

“Report a content error” opens a GitHub form in your browser, filled in with where you saw the error, the app version and the text on the screen. Nothing is sent unless you submit the form yourself. What you submit is public on GitHub and covered by GitHub’s privacy statement.
When this policy changes, the new version is published with a new date. For questions, use the developer email on Gil’s Google Play page.
